nameStory: Nodding spurge gets its name from its distinctive drooping flower clusters that seem to nod downward like sleepy heads. The 'spurge' part comes from the Latin 'spurgere,' meaning 'to purge,' referring to the family's historical use as a purgative medicine. It's also called 'eyebane' because the milky sap can cause serious eye irritation.
description: Nodding spurge is a low-growing annual weed that spreads in a sprawling, mat-like pattern across the ground. This small but persistent plant typically grows 6-12 inches tall and wide, with branching stems that radiate outward from a central point. Its tiny, inconspicuous flowers cluster together in small cups, and the entire plant has a somewhat succulent, fleshy appearance. Like all spurges, it bleeds a white, milky sap when broken.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats with stems that branch outward from the center like spokes of a wheel, often hugging the ground closely

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish-white flowers arranged in small cup-like clusters that characteristically droop or nod downward, especially noticeable in late summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged opposite each other along the stem, often with a slightly bluish-green color and smooth texture that feels somewhat thick and waxy

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Breaks stems to reveal thick, white milky sap that's sticky to touch and can stain fingers - be careful not to touch your eyes afterward

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, three-chambered seed capsules that split open when ripe, often making a tiny popping sound when squeezed gently

habitat: Look for nodding spurge in disturbed areas like sidewalk cracks, driveways, garden beds, and vacant lots throughout New England. It thrives in poor, compacted soils where other plants struggle and is particularly common in urban and suburban settings. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species in areas with foot traffic or vehicle disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with thick, waxy leaves, often appearing in the same spots where plants grew the previous year.
seasonality.summer: Plants spread into their characteristic mat-like form and begin producing their tiny, nodding flower clusters in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers mature into seed capsules and plants often turn reddish or purplish before dying with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Nodding spurge's seed capsules are like tiny botanical cannons - when they're ripe, they explosively shoot their seeds up to several feet away, which is how this little plant manages to colonize new sidewalk cracks and garden beds with such impressive efficiency.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with spotted spurge, but nodding spurge has drooping flower clusters (spotted spurge's flowers stand upright) and lacks the distinctive dark red spot in the center of each leaf that gives spotted spurge its name. Remember: nodding spurge nods down, spotted spurge has spots.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'weed,' nodding spurge is actually native to much of North America, including parts of New England, though it behaves like an invasive species in disturbed urban environments. The milky sap that all spurges produce can cause skin and eye irritation, so it's best to avoid handling these plants directly, especially around children and pets.
compareHints: Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters. Spotted spurge has similar growth but upright flowers and spotted leaves, while cypress spurge grows more upright with needle-like leaves. Petty spurge is more upright and branched, lacking the characteristic ground-hugging, radiating pattern of nodding spurge.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
